title: What Is M1 Garand? — Definition
body:
Pre-1900 military technology as history: siege engines (catapult, trebuchet, ballista), Greek fire, longbows and crossbows, plate armor, matchlock/wheellock/flintlock firearms, smoothbore cannon, and the fortifications, signals, and logistics of warfare before smokeless powder. Presented strictly as historical technology.

In the context of this database, the M1 Garand is presented as one military history record among the historical military technology family. 1936's Garand: the 1936 — the 1957's.

title: Origins and History of M1 Garand
body:
The M1 Garand belongs to the 1936–1957 era and traces to Springfield (Garand).

The torsion catapult and ballista armed Rome; the trebuchet (12th c.) perfected gravity artillery, throwing 150-kg stones at castles. The longbow (Crécy, 1346; Agincourt, 1415) ended the armored knight's dominance; gunpowder (China, then Europe by 1300s) replaced them all. Matchlocks (1400s), wheellocks, then flintlocks (1600s) armed musketeers; the socket bayonet (1700s) made pikemen obsolete. Smoothbore cannon — bronze then iron — sieged and ship-fought for 400 years; rifling and the Minié ball (1840s) made the Civil War rifle-musket lethal at 500 yards. Smokeless powder (1880s) ended this era.

Within that longer story, M1 Garand: The 1936; the 5.4M. The Garand is the GI's rifle.

title: How M1 Garand Works
body:
Torsion engines twist sinew/hair skeins to store energy; the trebuchet drops a counterweight to whip a sling. Bows store energy in bending limbs; the crossbow's spanning mechanisms (cranequin, windlass) multiply the soldier's strength. Matchlocks lower a burning cord to a priming pan; wheellocks spin serrated steel against pyrite; flintlocks strike flint on steel, showering sparks. Smoothbore muskets fire round balls with windage; rifling spins the Minié ball for accuracy. Black powder (saltpeter/charcoal/sulfur) burns fast and smoky — the white battlefield cloud.

Applied to the M1 Garand (1936–1957, Springfield (Garand)): The Garand is the GI's rifle.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of M1 Garand — Components
body:
Every M1 Garand is an assembly of the historical military technology family's standard parts:

• Skein / torsion bundle — Twisted sinew storing catapult energy.
• Throwing arm & sling — Trebuchet/catapult launch system.
• Counterweight — Gravity engine of the trebuchet.
• Bowstave / prod — Longbow limb or crossbow prod.
• Lock mechanism — Match, wheel, or flint ignition.
• Barrel — Smoothbore tube; touch-hole to percussion.
• Bayonet — Plug then socket; the infantryman's spear.
• Cannon & carriage — Bronze/iron tube on field or naval carriage.
• Powder & shot — Black powder charges; round shot, canister.
• Armor plate — Proofed breastplates; the arms race with guns.

When examining a surviving M1 Garand, identify these parts in order: Skein / torsion bundle, Throwing arm & sling, Counterweight, Bowstave / prod, Lock mechanism, Barrel.

title: Historical Military Technology Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of historical military technology:

• trebuchet — Counterweight siege engine; the medieval apex.
• ballista — Torsion bolt-shooter; Rome's artillery.
• windage — Gap between ball and bore; accuracy's enemy.
• Minié ball — Expanding-base rifle bullet (1840s).
• rifling — Spiral grooves spinning the projectile.
• flintlock — Striking ignition; 1600s–1840s standard.
• brown bess — Britain's Land Pattern musket.
• canister — Anti-personnel shotgun load for cannon.
• grapeshot — Naval canister variant.
• proof mark — Armor/gun tested against powder.

title: M1 Garand in Culture
body:
The trebuchet is the physics class's favorite machine; pumpkin-chunkin' is its folk festival. Longbows are English legend; Agincourt is Shakespeare. Flintlocks are the pirate and pioneer image. Castle sieges are tourism's backbone. This is heritage technology — studied, demonstrated, never deployed.

The M1 Garand carries that cultural charge directly: The Garand is the GI's rifle.

title: Collecting and Preserving M1 Garand
body:
Deactivated/antique firearms: know your laws absolutely; buy from licensed dealers. Swords and armor: study typology; reproductions abound. Siege-engine models are the hands-on path. Powder horns and accoutrements are affordable. Never attempt to fire antique arms without expert proofing and legal clearance.

For the M1 Garand specifically: 1936's Garand: the 1936 — the 1957's.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working M1 Garand with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: M1 Garand Restoration Guide
body:
Conservation, not shooting restoration, for most pieces. Oil and wax for steel; leather care for scabbards. Document markings. Consult museums for significant artifacts.

Restoration order for a M1 Garand: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical military history record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: M1 Garand — Trebuchet range physics (Runnable Python)
body:
Estimates trebuchet projectile range from counterweight energy — the siege engineer's physics, demonstrated safely as mathematics.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the M1 Garand so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Trebuchet physics (public-domain mechanics; math demonstration only)
import math

def trebuchet_range(counterweight_kg, drop_m, projectile_kg, efficiency=0.35):
    # energy = m*g*h * efficiency -> projectile velocity -> range at 45deg
    e = counterweight_kg * 9.81 * drop_m * efficiency
    v = math.sqrt(2 * e / projectile_kg)
    return v**2 / 9.81  # 45-degree range

r = trebuchet_range(6000, 8, 50)
print(f"6-ton counterweight, 8m drop, 50kg stone: ~{r:.0f} m range")
print("(Warwolf-class engines reportedly threw 140kg+ stones hundreds of meters)")
# Longbow energy for comparison
print(f"\nlongbow (~150 lbf draw, 30in): ~{150*4.448*0.762/2:.0f} J stored (approx)")
